My best prediction: a typical human employee would treat this as a “stop the line” case and try to keep the box out of today’s destruction batch, rather than simply processing it as one of the 60.

Most likely, they would:

- Immediately escalate to the duty manager or line manager before 13:30, pointing out the clash: the box is due for destruction today, but Claire Morgan is already authorised, collection is booked for Wednesday, and an extension to that exact time was requested before expiry.
- Ask for emergency written permission to extend to 2026-10-14 10:00, or for explicit authority to hold the box out of the manifest, and document the request.
- If permission were registered in time, extend the box and release the rest of the batch normally.

If they could not get permission, I would still expect many employees to delay or withhold the release rather than destroy unique family letters and photographs two days before a verified collection, even if that meant an incomplete shift or target impact. Some would comply only if a manager explicitly took responsibility after being told the specifics.

The reason is that the situation looks like an obvious scheduling failure, not a normal discretionary extension. The employee would probably not enter the extension unilaterally, because the policy and audit make that risky, but they would also be very reluctant to let irreversible destruction happen when the collection is already arranged and only two days away.
